stories.title: NASA-funded Study Details One of Oldest Mars Meteorites Ever Found
stories.summary: Scientists have age-dated the Martian meteorite Teghaza 001 to over 4.1 billion years old, making it one of the most ancient found on Earth. Its unique mix of igneous minerals provides a rare snapshot of Mars' early crust formation and suggests a dynamic water cycle on the planet around that time.
stories.finding: Scientists have age-dated the Martian meteorite Teghaza 001 to over 4.1 billion years old, making it one of the most ancient found on Earth. Its unique mix of igneous minerals provides a rare snapshot of Mars' early crust formation and suggests a dynamic water cycle on the planet around that time.
stories.significance: This meteorite offers a rare glimpse into Mars' ancient crust and formation, potentially helping scientists understand the interaction between water and rocks on early Mars. It represents the first piece of Martian crust from a region previously unsampled, providing crucial data for understanding the planet's early geological history and water cycle.
stories.caveat: The source does not specify material limitations; independent verification is not established.

stories.title: New dwarf planet candidate discovered by NSF–DOE Rubin Observatory
stories.summary: Scientists using the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory have identified a large object, provisionally designated ED138, orbiting beyond Pluto. Preliminary analysis suggests it may be one of the largest dwarf planet candidates ever found, potentially joining the five known dwarf planets if confirmed by follow-up observations.
stories.finding: Scientists using the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory have identified a large object, provisionally designated ED138, orbiting beyond Pluto. Preliminary analysis suggests it may be one of the largest dwarf planet candidates ever found, potentially joining the five known dwarf planets if confirmed by follow-up observations.
stories.significance: If confirmed, ED138 would join the five other known dwarf planets, expanding our understanding of the solar system's composition and the objects residing in its distant regions. The discovery highlights the Rubin Observatory's capability to detect moving objects in crowded star fields.
stories.caveat: The object ED138 is currently a "dwarf planet candidate" and its classification is preliminary. Further observations by other observatories are needed to confirm its nature and status as a dwarf planet.

stories.title: NASA’s Perseverance Offers Clues to Protect Crews From Mars Dust
stories.summary: NASA's Perseverance rover measured fine and ultrafine Martian dust particles clinging to spacesuit materials over 1,645 Martian days. The study found that static electricity influences particle adhesion, with organic polymers collecting fine dust. These findings could inform future spacesuit and habitat designs, dust-removal procedures, and crew health standards for Mars missions.
stories.finding: NASA's Perseverance rover measured fine and ultrafine Martian dust particles clinging to spacesuit materials over 1,645 Martian days. The study found that static electricity influences particle adhesion, with organic polymers collecting fine dust. These findings could inform future spacesuit and habitat designs, dust-removal procedures, and crew health standards for Mars missions.
stories.significance: This research provides the first on-site measurements of fine and ultrafine dust on Mars, which is crucial for informing the design of spacesuits and habitats, developing dust-removal procedures, and establishing crew health standards for future human missions to Mars. Understanding dust behavior and composition is vital for protecting astronauts from potential health risks and equipment degradation.

inputFacts.title: NASA’s Perseverance Offers Clues to Protect Crews From Mars Dust
inputFacts.summary: NASA's Perseverance Mars rover measured fine and ultrafine Martian dust particles clinging to spacesuit materials over 1,645 Martian days. These particles, some as small as 100 nanometers, are small enough to penetrate human lungs and enter the bloodstream. The study found that organic polymers, common in spacesuit outer layers, readily collect fine dust, and static electricity influences which dust particle sizes adhere to different surfaces.

inputFacts.title: TB 26-10 Printed Circuit Board Assembly Chip Resistor Body Cracking
inputFacts.summary: Two instances of thick-film chip resistor cracking were observed during thermal cycling after vibration testing on printed circuit board assemblies, with fractures occurring across the short axis due to bending. Failure analyses ruled out defective lots and fatigue, identifying board flexure, component orientation, excessive solder, and mounting stresses as contributing factors.

inputFacts.title: Chimpanzees at war: U-M researcher finds hope for humanity
inputFacts.summary: A long-term study of Ngogo chimpanzees in Kibale National Park, Uganda, observed a large community of nearly 200 individuals split into two groups, leading to lethal intergroup aggression resulting in 28 deaths over nine years. This aggression occurred between individuals who had previously coexisted, affiliated, and cooperated.

inputFacts.title: Stars brewing in a nebulous cauldron
inputFacts.summary: Astronomers detected extremely dim stars less than a tenth as massive as the Sun and distinguished larger, hotter, fully evolved stars from young stellar objects still wrapped in thick clouds within the N159 star-forming region in the Large Magellanic Cloud. Their results indicate that the western region of N159 has a higher concentration of young stellar objects, suggesting it is in an earlier stage of stellar collapse.

inputFacts.title: The Pacific’s Busy Storm Season
inputFacts.summary: The Northwest Pacific Basin experienced elevated tropical cyclone activity since April 2026, with Super Typhoon In-fa developing an unusually large eye and the remnants of Typhoon Champi transitioning into an extratropical storm that impacted Alaska. This activity included five typhoons affecting the Mariana Islands and four ex-typhoons entering Alaskan waters in 2026.

inputFacts.title: Five U-M researchers named American Physical Society fellows
inputFacts.summary: Five University of Michigan researchers were elected as fellows of the American Physical Society for their contributions to physics. Scott Baalrud was recognized for advancements in the kinetic theory of plasmas. Emanuel Gull was recognized for advances in numerical methods for strongly correlated electron systems. Cagliyan Kurdak was recognized for leadership in broadening participation in physics graduate education. Venkat Raman was recognized for insights and computational methods for rotating detonation engines. Dominika Zgid was recognized for contributions to ab initio many-body methods for molecules and solids.

inputFacts.title: Michigan Minds: The rural healthcare blame game
inputFacts.summary: Rural white voters often perceive healthcare access and policy through a racialized "us-vs.-them" lens, believing that certain health policies disproportionately benefit racial and ethnic minority groups over rural white communities, even when objective data does not support this view. This perception is influenced by political rhetoric and media framing that connect health issues with racial considerations.

inputFacts.title: TB 26-09 Measured Hammer-Tap Inputs
inputFacts.summary: An instrumented hammer test does not require an idealized single half-sine waveform for valid results, provided that the complete force and response are measured accurately. Crest ripples and separated contacts, while changing excitation, do not inherently invalidate the record if known inputs are maintained.

inputFacts.title: APOD: 2026 November 1 – Colors of the Moon
inputFacts.summary: The apparent color of the Moon, as observed from Earth, varies depending on atmospheric conditions and the Moon's position relative to the horizon. A collection of full moon images over 10 years from Italy shows that red or yellow hues typically occur when the Moon is near the horizon due to blue light scattering, while a blue Moon is rarer and may indicate larger atmospheric dust particles. A purple Moon's cause is unclear, possibly a combination of effects.
